replies.author: @o.j287
replies.text: ​​@kevinfromsales9445The truth is that Cuba is not under any kind of blockade. For instance, we in the Dominican Republic send 16 million eggs to Cuba annually, and the United States is one of its primary trading partners—in fact, most of the chicken meat consumed in Cuba comes from the U.S. The reality is that there is an embargo in place, which prevents U.S. companies from conducting business or operating in Cuba. This stems from the early days of the Cuban Revolution, when the government seized and expropriated a vast amount of U.S.-owned property without compensation—that is the reason for the embargo. However, the embargo does not apply to medicine, food, or other basic necessities. Transport vessels are permitted to reach Cuba, provided their route does not include the United States; for example, a ship could travel from the Dominican Republic to Cuba and then continue on to Nicaragua or elsewhere. What is prohibited is for a ship to travel from the Dominican Republic to Cuba and then proceed to the United States. While this complicates logistics, it does not mean that ships are barred from arriving in Cuba. In fact, the United States and several Western European nations—all U.S. allies—are among Cuba’s largest trading partners and conduct business there without issue. Furthermore, Cuba has specific types of stores where one can purchase the same kinds of goods found abroad, with the caveat that they must be paid for in U.S. dollars. Consequently, those who do not receive dollars from relatives abroad cannot purchase these items, while those who do receive such funds can. In short, there is no blockade; there is an embargo, and there are specific reasons for its existence.
